Strict, linear story, not an open-ended world Potion Permit iOS, Android $9.99 Earning a skeptical town’s trust over time Smaller cast, shorter story than Stardew Read more: 5 Best Mobile Games Like Tomodachi Life: Living the Dream 2026 Mobile Games Like Stardew Valley with Narrative-Driven Gameplay # These two life sim/RPG games like Stardew Valley go beyond farming to give you a town of characters whose stories run deeper the longer you stay. In Redbean , you write the stories yourself. In My Time at Portia, you discover them. Redbean # Platform: iOS, Android | Price: Free (optional IAP) Redbean is a free, cozy mobile sandbox where the town and everyone in it are yours to design. Traditional RPGs give you a preset story, Redbean gives you your own world. You create your own cast of characters, give each one a name, personality, and backstory, then place them in a pixel world you build from scratch. There are no heavy tasks like growing crops or selling stuff, and no seasonal deadline. You play at your own pace, build what you feel like, and let conversations unfold on your terms. What sets it apart is that the character and storyline are entirely yours . It puts players in an open-ended role-playing with in different storyline, you’re not dropped into a farm or world created by developers, but you’re the one to write stories yourself . Your towns can be a desert outpost, a beach, a medieval town, or anything else you’ve been imagining, and not limited to one. The characters hold conversations rooted in the lore and personality you’ve given them and respond in-character to NPCs – which are also yours, playing like a low-stakes RPG where you’re both the writer and one of the characters in the story. Redbean is a free life sim sandbox with custom pixel characters and player-designed towns, which can be a desert, coastal outpost, rural village, or anything you’ve pictured The honest gap: Redbean has no farming or crafting system, and Stardew’s romance storylines and marriage with pre-written NPCs haven’t been presented yet. Instead, what Redbean offers is the character authorship layer Stardew doesn’t have: a town of characters who are entirely yours from the start. Download Redbean Character Maker & Play Developer: Tinai Pvt. Ltd. Price: Free Download QR-Code Redbean: Character & Roleplay Developer: Tinai Pvt. Ltd. Price: Free My Time at Portia # Platform: iOS, Android | Price: $7.99 one-time purchase My Time at Portia puts you in a post-apocalyptic world that’s quietly rebuilding itself. You inherit your father’s run-down workshop in a small town. The game is partly about restoring it through crafting and commissions. Mostly, though, it’s about the community: a large NPC cast with distinct personalities and schedules, each with backstories that deepen the longer you stay. What it nails is relationship depth. For example, friendships develop through shared events, commissions, and gifts that reflect each character’s actual interests rather than generic item preferences. For players who lived for Stardew’s heart events and romance options, My Time at Portia runs on the same slow-burn rhythm with more cinematic delivery, like jealousy penalties and rivals. However, the iOS version hasn’t been updated since January 2022 and may have compatibility issues on recent devices. The crafting layer is also denser upfront than most NPC-focused players will expect. In contrast to the relaxing, play-at-your-own-pace rhythm in Stardew , Portia has timed main quests you need to complete with other builders, which bring a faster pace and a bit of competition. Mobile Games Like Stardew Valley with Deep NPC Relationships # Of all the mobile games like Stardew Valley on this list, these two focus most directly on the social layer itself, more about the daily rhythm of knowing a specific cast and watching how they shift over time. Wylde Flowers # Platform: iOS only (Apple Arcade) | Price: Included with Apple Arcade (~$6.99/month) Wylde Flowers is a farming and magic sim where the story carries more weight than the harvests. You play as Tara, who travels to the coastal town of Fairhaven to help her grandmother with the family farm, in a complicated community and a secret witches’ coven. The mystery unfolds through the relationships: a factional rivalry, romance options with genuine depth, and characters who reveal new layers the closer you get. Among mobile games like Stardew Valley here, Wylde Flowers is the one that nails the most in the emotional story and relatable characters: the island mystery gives each NPC arc a through-line that Stardew Valley’s character stories sometimes lack. It’s built for slow discovery, the story progresses at your own pace and the cozy life sim feel holds even when the narrative gets complicated. The limitation is firm: The game falls short in character creation and open-world experience like Stardew. Wylde Flowers is an Apple Arcade exclusive with no Android version. Still, if you’re on iPhone and already subscribe, it’s a solid option for mobile RPG games like Stardew Valley. Potion Permit # Platform: iOS, Android | Price: $9.99 Potion Permit starts with the town not wanting you there. You arrive in Moonbury as a chemist hired to treat the villagers, and the community is openly skeptical. Progress means earning trust through daily interactions, completed requests, and gifts that reflect what you’ve actually learned about each resident. Relationship-building feels like something that happened rather than something you unlocked. The potion-crafting loop (gathering ingredients, diagnosing ailments, brewing the right formula) is distinct from Stardew’s farming, and as a result it reads as a genuine alternative for players looking for games like Stardew Valley for Android or iOS with a different core loop entirely. Where it falls short: the cast is smaller than Pelican Town’s, and the main story arc resolves faster than most Stardew players expect. However, it works well as a focused weekend playthrough or a regular check-in game. Don’t go in expecting 100+ hours of NPC content. FAQ # Is Stardew Valley available on Android and iPhone? # Yes . Stardew Valley is available on both iOS and Android as a paid download ( $4.99 on App Store and Google Play). The mobile version covers the core game content. However, updates to the mobile ports have historically followed the PC version with a delay. Is there any free games similar to Stardew Valley? # There aren’t many free games similar to Stardew Valley with a genuine sim structure. Redbean is the closest option on this list, available on iOS and Android at no cost. For players who specifically want games like Stardew Valley but not farming, Redbean delivers the cozy, low-stakes feeling with complete creative freedom in creating your own stories and an open-ended RPG world. Any games like Stardew Valley without farming? # All four games here are better described as games like Stardew Valley but not farming in spirit. Instead of crops and seasons, the entire loop in Redbean is town-building and role-playing with your own characters, exploring endless stories and open-ended conversations. Potion Permit replaces farming with potion crafting and diagnosis mechanics. My Time at Portia and Wylde Flowers both include light farming as a side activity, but neither makes it the central loop. title: Mercury-Free Dental Fillings Gain Momentum as HHS Urges States to Phase Out Amalgam in Medicaid

body_text: HHS has urged states to phase out mercury-containing dental fillings in Medicaid programs by 2027. Learn what the policy means, why it matters, and how it could impact patients and providers. The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) has announced a major initiative encouraging states to eliminate the use of mercury-containing dental fillings within Medicaid programs. Through a notification sent by the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS), state Medicaid directors have been urged to restrict or discontinue coverage for dental amalgam procedures and transition toward mercury-free alternatives. The policy aligns with the federal government's broader health objectives and reflects growing concerns about the health and environmental impacts associated with mercury exposure. While the transition is expected to take place over the next few years, states have been encouraged to complete the phase out by 2027. What Are Mercury-Containing Dental Fillings? Dental amalgam has been used for more than 150 years to restore cavities. It is made by combining liquid mercury with metals such as silver, tin, and copper. Because of its durability and affordability, amalgam has long been a popular choice for treating tooth decay. However, advances in dental technology have made mercury-free materials, particularly resin-based composite fillings, more widely available. These alternatives closely match the natural color of teeth and are increasingly used in modern dentistry. Health officials say that the availability of these alternatives makes it possible to reduce reliance on mercury-containing materials while maintaining high standards of dental care. CMS Encourages States to Update Medicaid Coverage CMS has advised every State Medicaid Director to review dental coverage policies and consider limiting or ending reimbursement for dental amalgam procedures. Instead, states are encouraged to support the use of resin-based composite fillings whenever appropriate. The agency specifically referenced dental procedure codes associated with amalgam fillings and suggested replacing them with composite filling codes. According to CMS, most state Medicaid plans do not require formal amendments to implement these policy changes, making the transition administratively simpler. The guidance does not impose a federal mandate. Instead, it encourages states to voluntarily adopt policies that prioritize mercury-free dental treatments. Why Is Mercury a Concern? Mercury is recognized as a toxic heavy metal. Although dental organizations have generally maintained that dental amalgam is safe for most patients, public health agencies acknowledge that certain populations may be more vulnerable to mercury exposure. According to the CMS notification, groups that may face increased health risks include: Pregnant women Women planning pregnancy Children younger than six years old Individuals with neurological disorders People with impaired kidney function Other medically vulnerable populations Health officials believe reducing unnecessary exposure to mercury is an important preventive measure, especially when effective alternatives are available. Statements From Federal Health Officials HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. described the initiative as part of the administration's effort to modernize healthcare practices. According to Kennedy, mercury-containing dental materials are outdated given the widespread availability of safe and effective mercury-free options. He emphasized that taxpayer-funded healthcare programs should prioritize treatments that minimize exposure to potentially harmful substances. CMS Administrator Dr. Mehmet Oz also supported the initiative, stating that Americans should have confidence that healthcare systems promote the safest possible treatment options. He said encouraging Medicaid programs to move away from dental amalgam represents an important step toward improving patient care. Connection to the Indian Health Service Decision The CMS notification also reminded state officials that the Indian Health Service previously announced plans to stop using mercury-containing dental amalgam in its facilities by 2027. Federal officials said this earlier decision reflects increasing awareness of mercury's environmental impact and ongoing efforts to reduce its use throughout healthcare systems. The Indian Health Service serves millions of American Indians and Alaska Natives, making its policy shift an important milestone in the transition toward mercury-free dentistry. International Efforts to Reduce Mercury Use The United States is also participating in broader international efforts to reduce mercury use. CMS noted that the country is a party to the Minamata Convention on Mercury, an international treaty designed to protect human health and the environment from mercury pollution. Under commitments associated with the convention, participating countries aim to phase out the use of dental amalgam by 2034. Although individual countries may adopt different timelines and implementation strategies, the agreement signals growing global support for reducing mercury use across industries, including healthcare. What This Means for Medicaid Patients For most Medicaid beneficiaries, the transition is expected to increase access to mercury-free fillings rather than reduce dental services. Patients may increasingly receive composite resin fillings instead of amalgam when receiving treatment for cavities. Composite materials offer several advantages, including: Tooth-colored appearance Better cosmetic results Less removal of healthy tooth structure No mercury content Dentists will continue to evaluate which material is appropriate for each patient's clinical needs. Patients currently with amalgam fillings generally do not need to have them removed unless recommended by their dentist for medical or dental reasons. Potential Impact on Dentists and State Programs If states choose to follow CMS guidance, dental providers participating in Medicaid may gradually shift toward using composite materials for cavity restorations. State Medicaid agencies will need to review reimbursement policies, update billing guidance, and communicate changes to participating providers. Because CMS believes most states can implement these changes without submitting formal State Plan Amendments, officials expect the transition process to be relatively straightforward. Individual states will ultimately determine how and when they adopt the recommendations. The Broader "Make America Healthy Again" Initiative HHS described the phase out of mercury-containing dental fillings as part of the administration's broader "Make America Healthy Again" (MAHA) agenda. According to the department, the initiative seeks to modernize healthcare practices, reduce exposure to potentially harmful substances, and promote preventive health measures across federal health programs. Advancing mercury-free medical interventions has been identified as one component of these broader public health goals. Looking Ahead The CMS guidance marks another step in the ongoing shift away from mercury-containing dental materials in the United States. While states are not federally required to eliminate amalgam coverage immediately, many may begin reviewing their Medicaid dental policies over the coming months. As mercury-free materials continue to improve in durability, appearance, and affordability, experts expect their use to become increasingly common in both public and private dental care. The transition also aligns with international environmental commitments and reflects a broader trend toward minimizing unnecessary mercury exposure whenever suitable alternatives exist. Frequently Asked Questions Why is HHS encouraging states to stop using mercury dental fillings? HHS says mercury-free alternatives are widely available and reducing mercury exposure may improve health protection, particularly for vulnerable populations. Will existing mercury fillings need to be removed? No. Current guidance focuses on reducing the future use of dental amalgam rather than removing existing fillings. Patients should consult their dentist before considering replacement. What are the alternatives to dental amalgam? The primary alternative is resin-based composite filling material, which is mercury free and matches the natural color of teeth. Is the phase out mandatory? CMS has encouraged states to restrict or end Medicaid coverage for amalgam fillings, but implementation decisions remain with individual state Medicaid programs. When could the transition be completed? CMS has encouraged states to phase out the use of mercury-containing dental fillings by 2027, while international efforts under the Minamata Convention target a broader phase out by 2034. Source U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS). "Trump Administration Encourages States to End Mercury-Containing Dental Fillings." Official HHS news release. Disclaimer This article is intended for informational and educational purposes only. It summarizes information from an official U.S. Department of Health and Human Services announcement and should not be considered medical, dental, or legal advice. Patients should consult a qualified dentist or healthcare professional regarding treatment decisions. Policies described in this article may change, and implementation may vary by state.

title: 11 reasons your KYC verification is failing (and how to fix them)
summary: KYC verification failing? Here are the 11 most common reasons your check is rejected and exactly how to fix each one. Get verified faster today.
body_text: Seeing "KYC verification failed" doesn't necessarily mean your account has been rejected. More often, it means the verification system couldn't confirm your identity using the information or documents you submitted. The challenge is that providers don't always explain exactly what went wrong. As a result, many people keep uploading the same documents without fixing the underlying issue. Most KYC verification failures come from a small set of fixable mistakes, such as a blurry or expired ID, a name mismatch between your document and profile, poor lighting, an unsupported document type, or incorrect personal information. Once you've corrected the issue, you can usually pass verification on your next attempt. In this guide, we'll explain why your KYC verification is failing, how to resolve the most common issues, and what to do if your verification still doesn't go through. Most common KYC fixes at a glance Problem Quick fix Blurry ID photo Retake the photo in good lighting Expired document Upload a valid, unexpired ID Name doesn't match Make sure your profile exactly matches your ID Face verification fails Retake the selfie without hats or glasses Address doesn't match Upload a recent proof of address if required Unsupported document Check which IDs your provider accepts What does it mean when KYC verification fails? Know Your Customer (KYC) is the process financial companies use to confirm that you are who you say you are before giving you access to their services. To complete KYC, you'll usually be asked to provide information such as your full name, date of birth and address, along with a government-issued identity document. Many providers also require a selfie or short video to confirm that the person opening the account matches the identification provided. If your KYC verification failed, it doesn't usually mean you've been banned or that there's something wrong with your account. More often, it means the verification system couldn't confidently confirm your identity using the information or documents you submitted. Financial companies are required to carry out these checks to comply with anti-money laundering (AML) and financial crime regulations, helping protect both customers and the wider financial system. If you'd like to understand why these checks are necessary, read our guide on why KYC is required and how to do it easily. 11 reasons your KYC verification keeps failing Most KYC mistakes fall into a relatively small number of categories. Identifying the specific issue can save you time and help you avoid multiple failed attempts. 1. Your ID photo is blurry One of the most common causes of KYC failure is submitting an image that's difficult to read. If important details such as your name, date of birth or document number aren't clearly visible, the verification system may reject your submission automatically. How to fix it: Retake the photo in a well-lit area, keep your camera steady, and make sure the entire document is visible and in focus before uploading it. 2. Your identity document has expired Many providers only accept identity documents that are currently valid. Even if your passport or driving licence expired recently, it may no longer meet the verification requirements. How to fix it: Check the expiry date before uploading your document and use a current, valid form of identification. 3. Your name doesn't match your document Your profile information needs to match your identity document exactly. Even small differences, such as using a nickname, leaving out a middle name that's included on your ID, or making a spelling mistake, can cause your verification to fail. This is especially common if you've recently changed your name after marriage or another legal change but haven't updated all your documents. How to fix it: Double-check that the name on your account matches your identity document character for character before submitting your verification. 4. The lighting is too poor Even if your photo looks clear to you, shadows and low lighting can make it difficult for automated verification systems to read your document accurately. Dark images can also hide important security features that help confirm the document is genuine. How to fix it: Take the photo in bright, natural light whenever possible. Avoid dim rooms and make sure your entire document is evenly illuminated. 5. Glare is covering part of the document This is another issue that catches many people out. Bright reflections from overhead lights, camera flashes or sunlight can obscure text, photographs or security features, preventing the verification system from reading the document correctly. How to fix it: Turn off your camera flash, adjust the angle slightly and retake the photo until there's no glare covering any part of the document. 6. You're using an unsupported document Not every identity document is accepted by every financial provider. For example, one platform may accept national identity cards, while another only accepts passports or driving licences. Uploading the wrong document can result in an immediate rejection, even if it's perfectly valid. How to fix it: Check which identity documents your provider accepts before uploading your verification. If several options are available, choose the one that's easiest to photograph clearly. 7. Your proof of address doesn't match Some financial providers ask for proof of address in addition to your identity document. If the address on your utility bill, bank statement or other supporting document doesn't match the one you entered when creating your account, your verification may be rejected. This can also happen if you've recently moved house but haven't updated your records. How to fix it: Make sure the address on your application matches the address shown on your supporting document. If you've moved recently, use an accepted document that reflects your current address. 8. You don't meet the minimum age requirement Most regulated financial services require customers to be at least 18 years old, although the minimum age varies depending on the country and product. If the date of birth on your identity document shows that you don't meet the eligibility requirements, your KYC check won't be approved. How to fix it: Check the age requirements before applying. If you aren't eligible yet, you'll need to wait until you meet the minimum age. 9. You've created more than one account Many financial providers only allow one account per customer. Creating multiple accounts with the same personal information, email address, phone number or identity document can trigger security checks and prevent your verification from being completed. Sometimes this happens unintentionally because people forget they signed up previously. How to fix it: Try signing in to your existing account instead of creating a new one. If you can't access it, contact customer support before submitting another application. 10. Your internet connection interrupted the verification Identity verification relies on images and personal information being uploaded correctly. If your internet connection drops while documents or selfies are uploading, the files may be incomplete or corrupted, even if the upload appears to finish successfully. How to fix it: Use a stable Wi-Fi or mobile data connection and wait until every document has uploaded completely before closing the app or browser. 11. Your face doesn't match your identity document Many providers use facial recognition technology to confirm that the person opening the account is the same person shown on the identity document. Poor lighting, low image quality, wearing sunglasses or hats, or significant differences between your appearance and your ID photo can make it difficult for the system to verify your identity. How to fix it: Take your selfie in a well-lit area, remove anything covering your face, look directly at the camera and follow the instructions provided during the verification process. How to fix a failed KYC check step by step If your verification has been rejected, it can be tempting to upload the same documents again and hope for a different result. In most cases, you'll have a better chance of success by identifying the cause of the rejection first and correcting it before resubmitting your application. 1. Read the error message carefully Many providers explain why your verification failed, even if the message is brief. It might mention that your document couldn't be read, your face verification didn't match, or that some of your information was incorrect. Understanding the reason for the rejection will help you avoid making the same mistake again. 2. Review the information you submitted Compare the details on your application with your identity document. Check that your full name, date of birth and address match exactly, and confirm that you're using a valid, unexpired document. Even a small typo or a missing middle name can prevent your verification from being approved. 3. Retake your photos if needed If the issue relates to image quality, take new photos rather than uploading the same ones again. Use good lighting, place your ID on a flat surface, avoid reflections and make sure all four corners of the document are visible. If your provider requires a selfie, remove anything covering your face and look directly at the camera. 4. Submit your verification again Once you've corrected the problem, upload your documents again and wait for the verification process to complete. Avoid submitting multiple applications in quick succession unless you're instructed to do so, as repeated attempts can sometimes trigger additional security checks. 5. Contact support if the problem continues If you've reviewed your information, uploaded clear documents and your KYC verification still fails, contact customer support. Include any error messages you've received and explain the steps you've already taken. In some cases, the verification team can manually review your application or request additional documents to complete the process. Why legitimate customers sometimes fail KYC Receiving a failed KYC result doesn't mean you've done anything wrong. Modern verification systems rely heavily on automated document analysis and facial recognition. While these technologies are highly effective, they're not perfect. A legitimate customer can still fail verification because a document couldn't be read clearly, a selfie didn't meet the required quality, or the information provided couldn't be matched with enough confidence. Temporary technical issues can also affect the verification process. High demand, interrupted uploads or image processing errors may result in a failed check, even when all the information is correct. That's why it's important not to panic if your first attempt doesn't succeed. In most cases, reviewing the reason for the rejection, correcting the issue and submitting a new verification is enough to complete the process successfully. How long does KYC verification take? The time it takes to complete KYC verification depends on the financial provider, the documents you've submitted, and whether your application requires additional review. In many cases, automated verification is completed within a few minutes. If your documents are clear and all your information matches, you may be verified almost immediately. Some applications, however, take longer. A manual review may be required if the verification system can't confidently read your documents, your information needs to be checked more closely, or additional documents are requested. Delays are also more common during periods of high application volumes or if there's an issue with the images you've uploaded. If your verification has been pending for longer than the timeframe communicated by your provider, it's worth contacting customer support to check whether any further action is needed from you. How KYC works on Grey and how to pass it Like other regulated financial services, Grey uses KYC verification to help keep accounts secure and comply with financial regulations. Completing verification also helps protect customers by reducing fraud and preventing unauthorised account use. If you're completing your Grey KYC verification , the process is designed to be straightforward. You'll be asked to provide your personal information and upload the required identification documents. Depending on your country and the features you're applying for, you may also be asked to complete a face verification or provide additional documents. The easiest way to avoid delays is to make sure everything you submit is accurate the first time. Before uploading your documents, check that your name matches your identity document exactly, your ID is valid and easy to read, and your photos are taken in good lighting without reflections or cropped edges. If your verification doesn't go through on the first attempt, don't assume your account has been rejected. Review the reason provided, correct the issue, and submit your documents again. In many cases, a small change is all that's needed to complete the verification successfully. If you're opening your first Grey account, our guide on why KYC is required and how to do it easily explains the process in more detail and what to expect during verification. Once you're ready, you can open and verify a Grey account to access foreign currency accounts and international money transfers. To keep your account secure after you're verified, it's also worth reading our guides on protecting your Grey account from scams and fraud and whether Grey is legit and safe to use . Frequently asked questions What happens if I don't complete KYC verification? This depends on the provider, but you'll usually have limited access to your account until verification is complete. Some services won't allow you to send or receive money, while others may restrict certain features until your identity has been confirmed. Why do legitimate customers fail KYC? Most failed KYC checks are caused by document quality issues, incorrect information or automated verification systems being unable to confirm a person's identity with enough confidence. It doesn't necessarily mean there's anything wrong with your application. Can I use my account without completing KYC? Many regulated financial services require KYC before customers can access key features. Depending on the provider, you may be able to create an account, but you'll often need to complete verification before you can use services such as transfers, withdrawals or foreign currency accounts. Is my KYC information deleted after verification? Financial providers are generally required to retain customer verification records for a period defined by the regulations in the countries where they operate. The exact retention period varies depending on local legal requirements and the provider's policies. How many times can I retry KYC verification? The number of attempts varies between providers. Some allow several verification attempts before asking you to contact support, while others may temporarily pause further submissions after repeated failures. If you're unsure, it's best to review the provider's guidance or contact their support team before trying again. Can I complete KYC using a digital copy of my ID? Most providers require you to upload clear photographs or scans of an original, government-issued identity document. Whether digital identity documents are accepted depends on the provider and the country where you're verifying your account. Open a Grey account and get verified today A failed KYC check can be frustrating, but it doesn't usually mean you've reached the end of the process. In most cases, the issue comes down to something that can be corrected, such as unclear photos, information that doesn't match your documents, or an unsupported form of identification. Taking a few minutes to review your application before submitting it again can save you time and help you avoid repeated verification failures. If you're ready to manage money across borders, open a Grey account and get verified in minutes today .
